column1: What are the characteristic light microscopy findings in Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome (MCNS)?
column2: Normal glomeruli or a minimal increase in mesangial cells and matrix.

column1: What is the key electron microscopy feature of Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome (MCNS)?
column2: Diffuse effacement of the epithelial cell foot processes.

column1: What immunofluorescence pattern is typical for Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome (MCNS)?
column2: Typically negative for immune complex deposition.

column1: What proportion of children with Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome respond well to corticosteroid therapy?
column2: More than 90% of children.

column1: Which two clinical signs are classically absent in typical Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome?
column2: Hypertension and gross hematuria.

column1: In what percentage of Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome cases can microscopic hematuria be observed?
column2: Approximately 20% of cases.

column1: Which patient factors or clinical findings suggest a nephrotic syndrome diagnosis other than MCNS?
column2: Age under 1 year, positive family history, extrarenal signs (rash, arthritis, anemia), hypertension, gross hematuria, or renal insufficiency.

column1: What is the underlying etiology of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN)?
column2: Prior infection with nephritogenic strains of Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus.

column1: What is the peak pediatric age group for Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis?
column2: Children 5 to 12 years of age.

column1: What clinical manifestations constitute the classic presentation of acute glomerulonephritis?
column2: Preceding streptococcal infection, haematuria, edema, hypertension, and renal insufficiency (oliguria, raised creatinine).

column1: Why is renal biopsy NOT routinely performed when Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis is suspected?
column2: The diagnosis is primarily clinical; biopsy is reserved for atypical presentations or failure to recover as expected.

column1: Why is prednisolone contraindicated in the standard management of Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis?
column2: PSGN management is strictly supportive (fluid restriction, diuretics, antihypertensives); corticosteroid therapy is indicated for nephrotic syndrome, not PSGN.

column1: What mechanism causes blunting of costophrenic angles on plain chest radiograph in acute glomerulonephritis?
column2: Sodium and water retention lead to fluid overload, resulting in pleural effusions.

column1: 4-panel kidney biopsy findings in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis In panel D of these kidney biopsy findings, what characteristic electron microscopy structure is demonstrated?
column2: Subepithelial electron-dense deposits, commonly known as subepithelial humps.

column1: What immunofluorescence findings are seen on renal biopsy in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
column2: Bright granular capillary wall staining for complement C3 and IgG.

column1: What bacterial pathogen causes 80% to 90% of pediatric urinary tract infections?
column2: Escherichia coli.

column1: Outside the neonatal period, what is the predominant female-to-male ratio for urinary tract infections?
column2: 2:1 (females to males).

column1: Through what route do pathogens typically reach the kidneys in pediatric UTI after the neonatal period?
column2: Ascending spread of infection from the lower urinary tract (not hematogenous spread).

column1: Why is a urine WBC count $>10^5/\text{mL}$ an incorrect threshold for defining a UTI?
column2: The standard threshold of $>10^5$ refers to bacterial colony-forming units (CFU)/mL on culture, whereas pyuria (WBCs) is defined by much lower counts.

column1: What are the most common presenting symptoms of UTI in infants under 3 months of age?
column2: Fever, vomiting, lethargy, and irritability.

column1: What are the most common presenting symptoms of UTI in verbal children aged 3 years or older?
column2: Frequency and dysuria.

column1: According to NICE guidelines, what clinical factors define an Atypical UTI?
column2: Seriously ill child, poor urine flow, abdominal/bladder mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, failure to respond to suitable antibiotics within 48 hours, or non-E. coli infection.

column1: How is Recurrent UTI defined in pediatric guidelines?
column2: 2 or more episodes of upper UTI (pyelonephritis); OR 1 upper UTI plus 1 or more lower UTI (cystitis); OR 3 or more episodes of lower UTI.

column1: What is the first-choice oral antibiotic for UTI in children aged 3 months and over?
column2: Cefalexin.

column1: When is Co-amoxiclav indicated as a first-choice oral agent for pediatric UTI?
column2: Only when urine culture results are available and show specific susceptibility.

column1: Which intravenous antibiotics are recommended first-line for children with UTI who are vomiting or severely unwell?
column2: Cefuroxime, Ceftriaxone, Gentamicin, Amikacin, or Co-amoxiclav (in combination or if susceptible).

column1: What is the recommended timing for a DMSA scan following an atypical or recurrent UTI?
column2: 4 to 6 months following the acute infection.

column1: When is an ultrasound scan recommended during an acute UTI infection in infants younger than 6 months?
column2: When the infant has an atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, or fails to respond to treatment within 48 hours.

column1: DMSA scan showing differential renal function and MCUG image What is the primary purpose of obtaining a DMSA (dimercaptosuccinic acid) nuclear scan after pediatric pyelonephritis?
column2: To detect renal parenchymal defect/scarring and evaluate relative individual kidney function.

column1: Under what clinical conditions should a child with Diabetes Mellitus be admitted to the hospital?
column2: Very young age, inability of parents to monitor BGL, lack of supportive care at home, severe acute illness, or persistent ketonuria.

column1: What respiratory pattern is pathognomonic for severe Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)?
column2: Kussmaul respiration (rapid, deep, sighing respirations).

column1: What core clinical symptoms characterize Diabetic Ketoacidosis in children?
column2: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, nausea, frequent vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, tachypnea, acetone breath, and disordered sensorium.

column1: Why is blood glucose checking mandatory in a severely dehydrated child presenting with lethargy or confusion?
column2: Hypoglycemia is a deadly complication of acute illness/diarrhea; emergency triage rules dictate checking blood sugar or administering 10% dextrose for AVPU < A.

column1: Which two initial investigations must be ordered immediately for a severely dehydrated child with acute diarrhea and altered sensorium?
column2: Blood for urea, electrolytes, and creatinine; and blood glucose.

column1: What two initial laboratory tests are required to investigate suspected congenital hypothyroidism in a neonate?
column2: Serum Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) and Free T4.

column1: What is the mainstay medical treatment for congenital hypothyroidism?
column2: Thyroid hormone replacement therapy (Levothyroxine).

column1: At what intervals should serum Free T4 and TSH levels be monitored during medical management of pediatric hyperthyroidism?
column2: Every 1 to 3 months.

column1: What is the standard duration of antithyroid drug therapy in children before attempting a trial off treatment?
column2: 12 to 24 months.

column1: What percentage of children experience relapse within 2 years after completing antithyroid treatment?
column2: 40% to 75% of children.

column1: What treatment modalities offer permanent remission options following antithyroid drug relapse in children?
column2: Radioiodine treatment or subtotal thyroidectomy.

column1: What three physical facial signs define the classic 'Thalassemic facies' (chipmunk facies)?
column2: Prominent maxilla (enlarged cheekbones), depressed nasal bridge, and protruding upper teeth / frontal bossing.

column1: What single laboratory test provides definitive diagnostic confirmation for Beta-Thalassemia Major?
column2: Hemoglobin electrophoresis (or High-Performance Liquid Chromatography / HPLC).

column1: What hemoglobins are increased and decreased on Hb electrophoresis in Beta-Thalassemia Major?
column2: Increased HbF and markedly reduced or absent HbA.

column1: What pre-transfusion hemoglobin level must be maintained during chronic transfusion therapy for Beta-Thalassemia Major?
column2: Pre-transfusion $\text{Hb} > 9.5\text{--}10\text{ g/dL}$.

column1: Why is regular blood transfusion therapy mandatory in Beta-Thalassemia Major?
column2: To correct severe anemia, suppress ineffective erythropoiesis, and prevent skeletal bone deformities.

column1: At what serum ferritin threshold should iron chelation therapy be initiated in transfused Thalassemia patients?
column2: When serum ferritin reaches $1000\text{--}2000\ \mu\text{g/L}$ (usually after 10–20 blood transfusions).

column1: What procedure offers a curative option for patients with Beta-Thalassemia Major?
column2: HLA-matched allogeneic bone marrow transplantation.

column1: What red blood cell indices and parameters are seen on complete blood count in Beta-Thalassemia Major?
column2: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with reticulocytosis.

column1: Forearm showing petechial rash following tourniquet inflation How is the Hess test (tourniquet test) performed and interpreted?
column2: Inflate BP cuff to mid-way between SBP and DBP $\left(\frac{\text{SBP} + \text{DBP}}{2}\right)$ for 5 minutes. Count petechiae in a 1-inch square: $>20$ (or $>10$ in updated guidelines) is positive.

column1: What diagnostic specificity and pooled sensitivity does the Hess test possess for dengue diagnosis?
column2: Pooled sensitivity of 58% and specificity of 71%.

column1: During which days of fever is Dengue NS1 Ag testing most sensitive?
column2: The highest percentage of positive NS1 Ag tests occurs during the first 2 days of fever.

column1: What clinical features indicate Dengue warning signs during defervescence?
column2: Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, tender liver enlargement, and plasma leakage (ascites, pleural effusion).

column1: Which physical examination findings define dengue shock syndrome?
column2: Cold clammy extremities, tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure $(\le 20\text{ mmHg})$, or hypotension.

column1: What intravenous fluid choice is indicated during the critical phase of Dengue in infants younger than 6 months?
column2: Half-strength saline (isotonic fluids are used for infants $\ge 6$ months).

column1: What target hourly urine output confirms adequate fluid resuscitation in Dengue critical phase?
column2: Urine output $>0.5\text{ mL/kg/hour}$.

column1: Which criteria signal safe discontinuation of intravenous fluids in recovering Dengue patients?
column2: Absence of fever for 48 hours without antipyretics, clinical improvement (good appetite, normal hemodynamics, no respiratory distress), rising platelet trend, and stable hematocrit.

column1: Which clinical signs correlate with increasing severity of pediatric respiratory distress?
column2: Inability to take feeds/food, respiratory rate $>40/\text{min}$, altered mental state, and intercostal retractions.

column1: Why is high fever alone NOT a reliability indicator for severity of respiratory distress?
column2: Fever indicates systemic infection/inflammation but does not directly quantify work of breathing or impending respiratory failure.

column1: Which pediatric respiratory conditions characteristically present with wheezing on examination?
column2: Asthma, bronchiolitis, and foreign body inhalation.

column1: Why are acute laryngitis and tonsillitis excluded from the differential diagnosis of lower airway wheezing?
column2: Acute laryngitis presents with inspiratory stridor and hoarseness, while tonsillitis presents with stertor and sore throat; neither causes intrathoracic expiratory wheezing.

column1: What is the peak age group affected by Acute Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup)?
column2: Between 6 months and 3 years of age.

column1: What first-line pharmacotherapy effectively treats Croup (ALTB)?
column2: Oral Dexamethasone.

column1: What emergency nebulized treatment is used as a time-buying measure before intubation in severe Croup?
column2: Nebulized L-adrenaline (1:1,000 solution).

column1: What heart rate threshold defines Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) in infants and young children?
column2: Heart rate $>180\text{--}220/\text{min}$ in infants and children (typically $>160/\text{min}$ in older individuals).

column1: What characteristic ECG abnormality is seen in pediatric SVT?
column2: P waves are absent, retrograde, or obscured within preceding T waves.

column1: Why does pediatric SVT with chest pain require hospital admission and continuous monitoring?
column2: SVT can precipitate acute heart failure and myocardial ischemia, requiring telemetry monitoring and antiarrhythmic intervention.

column1: What medical conditions form the differential diagnosis of generalized peripheral edema in children?
column2: Acute glomerulonephritis, Nephrotic syndrome, Heart failure, and Cirrhosis of the liver.

column1: Why is angioedema differentiated from general pitting edema in systemic disorders?
column2: Angioedema causes transient, asymmetric localized subcutaneous swelling without gravitational pitting edema.

column1: What three main reasons justify combination drug therapy in pediatric HIV and Tuberculosis infections?
column2: To increase clinical effectiveness, reduce individual drug side effects, and prevent drug resistance.

column1: Why is empiric broad-spectrum combination antibiotic therapy indicated when causal organisms are unknown in severe neonatal sepsis?
column2: Empiric coverage (such as Ampicillin plus Gentamicin) covers both Gram-positive and Gram-negative neonatal pathogens, providing lifesaving synergy before culture results arrive.

column1: Why do drug dosages of the same therapeutic agent vary significantly across different pediatric diseases?
column2: Dosing depends on the pathophysiological target (e.g., low-dose Prednisolone for mild asthma anti-inflammation vs high-dose Prednisolone for nephrotic syndrome immunosuppression).

column1: What is the recommended management for a child presenting with simple mild Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA vasculitis) rash and normal urinalysis?
column2: Clinical diagnosis with outpatient monitoring (urine dipstick for proteinuria and blood pressure monitoring for hypertension); most cases resolve spontaneously without intervention.

column1: When is hospital admission required for a child with Henoch-Schönlein Purpura?
column2: When severe renal complications (nephritic/nephrotic signs) or severe abdominal complications (severe pain, bleeding, intussusception) develop.

column1: Diagram of renal corpuscle detailing Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, afferent arteriole, and efferent arteriole Which arteriole carries unfiltered blood directly into the glomerular capillary tuft?
column2: The Afferent Arteriole.

column1: What anatomical structure surrounding the glomerular tuft receives the ultrafiltrate before it enters the proximal convoluted tubule?
column2: Bowman's Capsule.
